column1: What does a Database Transaction Unit (DTU) measure in Azure SQL Database?
column2:
A blend of CPU, memory, and read/write I/O resources.
A DTU combines several resources into one capacity measure. Choosing a DTU size increases the bundle rather than letting you choose CPU, memory, or I/O independently.
Review source

column1: Why does the vCore model help with capacity planning for an on-premises SQL Server migration?
column2:
It exposes CPU and memory capacity more directly.
A vCore represents a virtual CPU. The model exposes the number of vCores and the memory available with the chosen hardware, which makes comparison with the source workload easier.
Review source

column1: Which Azure SQL Database vCore tier targets a balanced budget and uses remote storage for database files?
column2:
General Purpose.
General Purpose separates the compute that runs queries from remote storage for database files. Replacement compute can reattach the files after a failure. The tradeoff is higher storage latency than local SSD storage.
Review source

column1: What storage architecture gives Business Critical low I/O latency?
column2:
Locally attached SSD storage on the compute nodes.
Business Critical keeps database files on SSDs attached to the compute nodes. The shorter storage path helps I/O-intensive work, but query waits and application delays still affect total transaction time.
Review source

column1: Which Business Critical feature lets read-only reports use a secondary replica instead of the primary?
column2:
Read scale-out to an included read-only secondary.
Read scale-out lets a read-only connection route reporting work to a secondary replica. The secondary uses separate compute, so the primary can focus on the main workload.
Review source

column1: Which Azure SQL Database service tier supports a single database up to 128 TB?
column2:
Hyperscale.
Hyperscale supports up to 128 TB of data in one database. General Purpose and Business Critical have lower limits, and their supported storage can depend on the selected compute size.
Review source

column1: Which components serve database pages to Hyperscale compute replicas?
column2:
Page servers.
Page servers supply database pages to the compute replicas. This separation lets the service scale compute independently rather than moving the entire database each time compute changes.
Review source

column1: What storage amount determines Hyperscale data storage charges?
column2:
Allocated data storage, rather than the maximum supported database size.
Allocated storage is the data space reserved for the database files, including space not yet used by rows. Hyperscale bills this allocation rather than billing all the way up to its supported maximum.
Review source

column1: Which Hyperscale replica type supports independently sized read-only workloads?
column2:
A named replica.
A named replica can have a different compute size from the primary. For example, a reporting workload can use a separate read-only replica sized for its own needs.
Review source

column1: How is provisioned compute billed when an Azure SQL Database is idle?
column2:
The provisioned compute capacity remains billable at its hourly rate.
Provisioned compute stays available at the selected size even when no queries run. The bill reflects that capacity rather than the CPU seconds the workload actually used.
Review source

column1: Which Azure SQL Database compute tier automatically scales compute for intermittent demand?
column2:
Serverless.
Serverless adjusts compute as demand changes, within the configured range. This suits workloads with idle periods and bursts because they do not always need the capacity required at peak demand.
Review source

column1: How does Azure SQL Database calculate compute charges for each active second of a serverless database?
column2:
Per second, using the higher of CPU usage and normalized memory usage, subject to minimums.
The service compares CPU use with memory expressed in vCores and applies configured minimums. For example, 6 GB of memory counts as 2 vCores for billing. The larger value can determine the bill.
Review source

column1: Which charges continue while an Azure SQL Database serverless database is paused?
column2:
Storage charges.
Storage remains allocated during a pause, even though no compute is billed. An idle database that has not actually paused can still incur the minimum compute charge.
Review source

column1: What serverless delay matters when the first request after inactivity must respond quickly?
column2:
Compute warm-up or resume delays.
An auto-paused database must resume before it can serve work, and inactive serverless compute can also need time to warm up. Consider provisioned compute if the first request must respond promptly.
Review source

column1: What does MAXDOP limit inside a SQL Server query plan?
column2:
The maximum degree of parallelism for individual parallel operations in a query plan.
MAXDOP limits the degree of parallelism for individual parallel operations in a plan. One query can contain several such operations, so MAXDOP is not a cap on all workers for the query.
Review source

column1: Why does Microsoft recommend avoiding MAXDOP 0 in Azure SQL Database?
column2:
Excess parallelism can starve concurrent queries of CPU and worker resources.
MAXDOP 0 does not impose a configured degree limit. A parallel query can then compete for many workers and CPU resources. Test changes with several queries running together, not just one query alone.
Review source

column1: Which Azure SQL automatic tuning option can restore a previously good plan after a regression?
column2:
FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN.
This option uses Query Store history to identify a plan change that hurt performance. It can force a previously better plan, then evaluate the result. Inspect the effective tuning configuration rather than assuming it is enabled.
Review source

column1: Which Azure SQL Database automatic tuning option creates indexes and checks their performance benefit?
column2:
CREATE_INDEX.
CREATE_INDEX lets Azure SQL Database apply eligible index recommendations and measure the result. Under Azure SQL Database defaults it is off. Azure SQL Managed Instance does not support this tuning option.
Review source

column1: Which Azure SQL Database automatic tuning option removes eligible unused or duplicate indexes?
column2:
DROP_INDEX.
DROP_INDEX can remove duplicates or indexes that qualify as unused. It protects unique indexes. On Premium and Business Critical it removes only eligible duplicates, not indexes merely classified as unused.
Review source

column1: What happens when an automatically applied tuning change fails performance validation?
column2:
The service reverts the change.
The service measures performance after applying the recommendation. If it does not observe an improvement, it reverses its automatic change instead of leaving the change in place without evidence.
Review source

column1: What validation is missing when you manually run a tuning recommendation's T-SQL script?
column2:
The automatic performance validation and reversal workflow.
Running the script makes the change without the service managing its outcome. Measure performance before and after the change, and undo it yourself if it harms the workload.
Review source

column1: What happens to an existing Azure SQL database's compatibility level when Microsoft introduces a newer default?
column2:
It keeps its existing level until someone changes it.
A compatibility level controls selected SQL and optimizer behavior. A newer default applies to new databases and does not change an existing database's setting. Plan and test a change separately.
Review source

column1: Which feature captures a query performance baseline before a compatibility-level upgrade?
column2:
Query Store.
A baseline is a set of measurements from before the change. Query Store keeps those measurements and the associated plans. Compare them with performance after raising the compatibility level.
Review source

column1: Which database-scoped configuration reduces cache memory consumed by single-use ad hoc plans?
column2:
OPTIMIZE_FOR_AD_HOC_WORKLOADS.
An ad hoc batch is SQL submitted outside a stored procedure. If many different batches run only once, this setting saves cache memory by storing a small stub for each new batch instead of its full plan.
Review source

column1: With ad hoc optimization enabled, what is cached after an ad hoc batch's first compilation?
column2:
A small compiled plan stub instead of the full compiled plan.
On the first execution, the plan runs but only a small stub is cached. If the same batch runs again while its stub remains cached, SQL Server compiles the plan again and caches the full plan.
Review source

column1: Which database engine feature speeds recovery and rollback involving long-running transactions?
column2:
Accelerated database recovery (ADR).
Accelerated database recovery (ADR) keeps persistent row versions. These versions let the engine undo many row changes without working backward through all of a long transaction's log history in the traditional way.
Review source

column1: What is the default enablement state of accelerated database recovery (ADR) in Azure SQL Database?
column2:
Always enabled.
Azure SQL Database provides ADR as part of the service. Customers do not need to turn it on and cannot turn it off. Do not assume installations of SQL Server use the same default.
Review source

column1: Where does Azure SQL Database store the row versions used by accelerated database recovery (ADR)?
column2:
Inside the user database, not tempdb.
The persistent version store holds row versions that ADR needs for recovery. In Azure SQL Database it consumes space inside the user database, whether versions are stored in the affected row or separately.
Review source

column1: How does accelerated database recovery (ADR) affect log truncation during a long-running transaction?
column2:
It permits aggressive log truncation despite active long-running transactions.
Persistent versions reduce the log history needed to undo many changes. An active transaction therefore does not have to hold back truncation in the same way, although other conditions can still delay it.
Review source

column1: What additional work can accelerated database recovery (ADR) add to a write-heavy workload?
column2:
Row versions need additional data space and transaction logging.
Keeping persistent versions adds data and logging work when rows change. Versions stored in rows can also make those rows larger and increase page splits. Measure the effect on the actual write workload.
Review source

column1: Why can long transactions increase storage use even when accelerated database recovery (ADR) speeds up rollback?
column2:
Long-running transactions can delay version cleanup and increase PVS size.
ADR can speed up undo but does not make long transactions free. Old versions can remain necessary while a transaction is open, increasing space use until the cleaner can remove them.
Review source

column1: Which dynamic management view reports ADR persistent version store metrics?
column2:
sys.dm_tran_persistent_version_store_stats.
This view gives persistent version store metrics for each database. Its size column counts off-row versions only, so the reported value does not measure storage consumed by versions kept inside data rows.
Review source

column1: What determines the default compatibility level for newly created databases in Azure SQL Managed Instance?
column2:
The instance's update policy.
The update policy determines which engine feature set the instance tracks. That policy affects the default compatibility level for newly created databases. Inspect the actual database setting rather than inferring it from the service name.
Review source

column1: Which automatic tuning option creates indexes by default in SQL database in Microsoft Fabric?
column2:
CREATE_INDEX.
Fabric SQL database enables automatic index creation by default. It uses workload evidence to select and assess indexes. Do not assume the same default applies to Azure SQL Database.
Review source
